items.title: 0.9999... equals 1, exactly
items.claim: The decimal expansion 0.999... (infinitely many 9s) does not approach 1 — it IS 1. Two different decimal expansions can represent the same real number.

options.text: They're approximately equal but slightly different
They have zero difference (1 - 0.999... = 0); 0.999... = sum of 9/10 to the n for n from 1 to infinity = 9/10 / (1 - 1/10) = 1 exactly

items.reveal:
Every infinite decimal expansion is, by definition, a convergent series.
0.999... = 9/10 + 9/100 + 9/1000 + ...
     = 9/10 * (1 + 1/10 + 1/100 + ...)
     = 9/10 * 1/(1 - 1/10)
     = 9/10 * 10/9
     = 1

Another argument: let x = 0.999... Then 10x = 9.999... Subtract: 10x - x = 9.999... - 0.999... so 9x = 9 and x = 1.

Third argument: the difference 1 - 0.999... is less than 10 to the minus n for every n. The only non-negative real with this property is 0. So 1 - 0.999... = 0 and 0.999... = 1.

Decimals are a representation, not an identity. Any real with a terminating decimal also has a 999...-style alternative: 0.5 = 0.4999..., 1 = 0.999..., 0.123 = 0.122999... The two representations are equal.

In educational settings this is one of the most strongly contested results — students often refuse to accept it. The objection is usually based on confusing representations with the numbers themselves.
items.why: Decimals feel like unique addresses for numbers. They are not — every terminating decimal has a recurring-9 twin, and equality of the two is logically forced.

items.title: A bottle with no inside
items.claim: A normal bottle has an inside and an outside, separated by the bottle wall. The Klein bottle has no inside. There is only one surface — what looks like 'inside' is connected to 'outside' through the surface itself.
items.prompt: How is the Klein bottle different from a regular surface?

options.text: It's non-orientable — there is no consistent way to assign 'outward normals'; a left-handed walker traversing it can come back as right-handed
It's actually two surfaces glued together
Klein bottles only exist in imagination

items.reveal:
Klein constructed the bottle as a 2D analogue of the Möbius strip — but closed. To build one in 3D, you must let the bottle 'pass through itself' (a fake self-intersection). Properly, it lives in 4-dimensional space, where it has no intersection.

In rigorous terms: the Klein bottle is a non-orientable, closed 2-manifold with Euler characteristic 0. It cannot be embedded in 3D Euclidean space without self-intersection.

The Möbius strip (Möbius, 1858) is a 2D example with boundary: cut one open and you get a long strip; cut it in half lengthwise and you get a single longer Möbius strip, not two.

Non-orientable surfaces matter in physics (some condensed matter systems behave like Möbius strips), engineering (conveyor belt design uses Möbius topology to wear evenly), and cosmology (toy models of non-orientable universes have been considered, though our universe seems to be orientable).
items.why: 3D objects have an obvious inside and outside. Topology shows some 2D surfaces don't — the apparently obvious 'inside/outside' distinction is a special feature of orientable manifolds.

items.title: The simplest population equation in the world becomes chaotic
items.claim: Logistic map: x_(n+1) = r * x_n * (1 - x_n). At r = 2.5, x converges to a fixed point. At r = 3.2, it oscillates between two values. At r = 3.7, the values look random. The system is deterministic but unpredictable.

options.text: Nothing — the system is always periodic

Period-doubling cascade: a single fixed point splits into a 2-cycle, then a 4-cycle, then 8, 16, 32... at geometrically closer values of r (Feigenbaum's constant ~4.669). Beyond ~3.5699, the system becomes chaotic
Only mathematicians can see the difference
The chaos is a calculation error

items.reveal_title: Period doubling and the road to chaos
items.reveal:
The logistic map x_(n+1) = r * x_n * (1 - x_n) was introduced by Robert May (1976) as a simple model of population growth with carrying capacity.

For r between 0 and 1: x converges to 0.
For r between 1 and 3: x converges to a non-zero fixed point.
At r = 3: the fixed point becomes unstable; period-2 cycle appears.
At r ≈ 3.449: period-4 cycle appears.
At r ≈ 3.544: period-8.
At r ≈ 3.5644: period-16.

The period-doublings occur at geometrically closer r-values, with ratio approaching Feigenbaum's constant delta ≈ 4.669 — a universal constant of period-doubling bifurcations, appearing in many physical systems (dripping faucet, electronic circuits, fluid dynamics).

At r ≈ 3.5699: 'Edge of chaos'. Beyond this, the system becomes chaotic — small differences in initial conditions grow exponentially.

Within the chaos there are 'islands of stability' (e.g., a period-3 window near r ≈ 3.83). The bifurcation diagram has fractal structure.

This system shows that deterministic dynamics can produce apparent randomness. It motivated chaos theory in the 1970s-80s.

Applications:
- Population biology (when not too realistic).
- Cryptography (pseudo-random number generators).
- Modelling complex systems (transitions to turbulence).
- Analogies to neural and economic dynamics.

The logistic map is a foundational example in the study of dynamical systems and has become a textbook reference for chaos.
items.why: Even the simplest equations can produce unpredictable behaviour. Determinism doesn't guarantee predictability — chaos can emerge from one-line iterations. This insight overturned 19th-century certainty about Newtonian mechanics.
